name: Ironclad Agrisystems Mycelial Anchor Net
description:
The Mycelial Anchor Net is a deployable load-bearing climbing and rigging system derived from Ironclad Agrisystems' proprietary engineered fungal fiber technology, originally developed for vertical hydroponic tower structures in GLMZ's upper-district agricultural zones. The kit consists of a compressed deployment canister containing 80 meters of mycelium-composite fiber rope, six hardened anchor bolts with self-expanding fungal root heads, and a tension management spool with integrated load sensor. When the anchor bolts are driven into porous surfaces — concrete, brick, compressed earth, or soft stone — the root heads are activated by a saline charge, expanding into the surrounding material over 40 seconds and forming a mechanical interlock that exceeds the tensile strength of the fiber itself.

The fiber rope is Ironclad's most commercially visible innovation: a braided composite of engineered mycelium strands and carbon nanotube reinforcement that achieves a tensile strength of 2.4 tonnes at 6mm diameter while remaining flexible at temperatures down to -30°C. Unlike synthetic polymer ropes, the mycelial composite absorbs minor abrasion and micro-fractures through a passive self-repair process that continues for up to 14 days after deployment, provided ambient humidity is above 30%. The rope has a distinctive dark grey-green coloration and a faintly organic texture that makes it immediately recognizable to anyone familiar with Ironclad's product line.

The Mycelial Anchor Net was not designed for infiltration use, but it has been enthusiastically adopted by GLMZ's vertical-movement community — climbers, building runners, and extraction teams operating in the city's dense upper-district tower clusters. Ironclad has made no effort to restrict access, viewing field adoption by runners as effective advertising for their agricultural and construction clients.

specifications.anchor_compatible_surfaces: Porous concrete, brick, compressed earth, soft stone

tactical_use: Primary use is rapid vertical ascent or descent on building exteriors, particularly in the tower clusters of the upper districts where conventional grapple points are minimal. The self-expanding anchors are preferred over driven pitons in noise-sensitive operations because the saline activation produces no percussive sound. The load sensor integration allows a team to monitor anchor integrity in real time during a suspended operation.
cultural_context: The MAN has a curious dual identity in GLMZ. In the upper districts, it's sold openly at agricultural supply depots and building maintenance outlets, marketed to tower garden technicians and facade maintenance crews. In the lower districts and the vertical slum stacks of the mid-ring, it's a prestige item among building runners — the distinctive grey-green rope has become a visual shorthand for someone who does serious vertical work. Knockoff versions using standard synthetic fiber dyed to match are common enough that experienced runners have learned to test rope samples before trusting their weight to them.
story_hooks: A runner finds a length of Mycelial Anchor rope still attached to a high-rise anchor point — the other end disappears into a sealed window three floors below, and the rope is still in its self-repair phase, meaning it was deployed within the last two weeks.

Ironclad's agricultural division is quietly investigating who has been bulk-purchasing MAN kits through shell companies — the quantities suggest someone is rigging an entire building, not just making an access run.
A counterfeit MAN kit fails during a job, and the runner who survives the fall wants to find whoever is flooding the market with fakes.
A corporate tower's security upgrade includes a surface treatment that prevents mycelial root expansion — someone sold the anchor's biological vulnerability to a competitor.
